subject: Chemistry
title: States of Matter and Phase Changes
learningOutcomes: Define chemistry as the study of matter, its properties, composition and interactions, or as the study of earth (solids), air (gases), sea (liquids) and sky (plasma).
Explain with examples that chemistry has many branches: physical, inorganic, organic, environmental, analytical, bio-, nuclear, polymer, geo-, medicinal and astrochemistry.
Define matter as a substance having mass and occupying space.
State the distinguishing properties of solids, liquids and gases, such as density and compressibility.
Describe plasma, intermediate states (supercritical fluid, liquid crystal, graphene) and exotic states of matter.
Explain allotropy and the allotropic forms of carbon, sulphur and oxygen.
Explain the difference between elements, compounds and mixtures.
Identify solutions, colloidal solutions and suspensions as mixtures and give an example of each.
Explain unsaturated and saturated solutions and the effect of temperature on solubility.

sections.heading: What Chemistry Studies
sections.body: Chemistry is the branch of science which deals with the properties, composition and structure of substances. It also deals with the physical and chemical changes in matter and the laws which govern these changes. Composition means the percentages of elements and compounds in a sample of matter, and structure means the arrangement of atoms in matter. Physical and chemical changes may be brought about by absorption or evolution of energy. Chemistry can also be described as the study of earth (solids), air (gases), sea (liquids) and sky (plasma) and their interaction.

sections.heading: The Eleven Branches of Chemistry
sections.body: Chemistry is divided into branches so that scientists can focus on distinct areas. Physical chemistry studies how substances behave at atomic and molecular levels and how reaction rates can be predicted and changed. Inorganic chemistry deals with elements and compounds containing little or no carbon, while organic chemistry deals with carbon compounds such as hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Environmental chemistry studies pollution; analytical chemistry separates, identifies and measures the components of a material; biochemistry studies the chemical processes of living organisms. Nuclear chemistry deals with reactions in the nucleus, polymer chemistry with large molecules made from building blocks, geochemistry with the composition of Earth, medicinal chemistry with the design of drugs, and astrochemistry with molecules and ions in space.

sections.heading: States of Matter
sections.body: Matter is anything other than energy that has mass and occupies space; energy is non-material. Solid, liquid and gas are the three primary states, and they differ in the strength of intermolecular forces, the arrangement of particles and the distance between them. Gas molecules are very widely apart with very weak forces, so gases are easily compressible with very low density. Liquid molecules are closely attached but move randomly, with significant forces. Solid particles oscillate about fixed positions with very strong attractions, so a solid has a definite shape and fixed volume and is the only state that needs no container. Plasma, the fourth state, is a partially ionized gas found in fluorescent tubes, lightning and welding arcs; supercritical fluids, liquid crystals and graphene are intermediate states, and dark matter and Bose–Einstein condensate are exotic states.

sections.heading: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
sections.body: An element is the simplest form of matter; it contains the same kind of atoms and cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical reactions. A compound is made of two or more different elements combined in a fixed ratio, for example hydrogen and oxygen in water in the ratio 1 : 8 by weight, and its properties differ from those of its elements. A mixture is formed when elements or compounds are mixed in any ratio; each component keeps its own properties and can be separated by physical methods. A mixture with uniform concentration throughout is homogeneous and one with different concentrations in different parts is heterogeneous.

sections.heading: Allotropy
sections.body: The existence of an element in more than one structural form is called allotropy, and the different forms are allotropic forms. Carbon exists as diamond (giant macromolecular structure), graphite (layers of hexagonal rings) and Buckminster fullerene C₆₀ (spheres of pentagons and hexagons). Oxygen exists as O₂ and ozone O₃. Sulphur exists in two crystalline forms, rhombic and monoclinic, of which rhombic is the more stable.

sections.heading: Comparing Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
sections.body: Elements are represented by symbols such as Na and Ca, while compounds are represented by formulae. A compound can be broken into its elements only by a chemical reaction, but a mixture can be separated by physical methods. Gaseous elements such as nitrogen, oxygen and chlorine exist as independent molecules, whereas noble gases like helium and argon are mono-atomic. Compounds such as hydrogen chloride, ammonia and water exist as molecules, while sodium chloride and sand exist as network arrangements.

sections.heading: Solutions, Colloids and Suspensions
sections.body: Mixtures usually exist as true solutions, colloidal solutions or suspensions. In a true solution, such as sodium chloride or copper sulphate in water, the solute particles are completely homogenized and cannot be seen; they pass through filter paper and leave no residue. A colloidal solution, such as starch solution or the white of an egg, has particles a little bigger which do not settle down yet pass through filter paper. In a suspension, such as chalk in water, the particles do not dissolve, can be seen, settle down on standing and are left as a residue on filter paper.

sections.heading: Saturated and Unsaturated Solutions
sections.body: When sugar is added to water in small portions it dissolves at first, giving an unsaturated solution that can dissolve more solute. At one stage no more sugar dissolves and the extra settles at the bottom; this is a saturated solution, which holds the maximum amount of solute at that temperature. The solubility of a solute is the amount which can dissolve in 100 g of a solvent at a particular temperature. At 20 °C, 36 g of sodium chloride but 203.9 g of table sugar dissolve in 100 g of water.

sections.heading: Temperature and Solubility
sections.body: Usually the solubility of solids increases as temperature rises, but this is not a general rule. KNO₃, AgNO₃, KCl, CuSO₄ and NaNO₃ become more soluble when heated; NaCl shows no appreciable increase; and Li₂CO₃, CaCrO₄ and Ca(OH)₂ become less soluble. The solubility of gases in water decreases with an increase in temperature, so soda-water bottles are kept in a refrigerator to keep carbon dioxide dissolved longer. Because many solids dissolve more in hot water, a solid can be purified by dissolving it in hot water and cooling to obtain pure crystals.

definitions.definition: The branch of science that deals with the properties, composition and structure of substances and the changes in matter.
The percentages of elements and compounds in a sample of matter.
The arrangement of atoms in matter.
Anything other than energy that has mass and occupies space.
One of the distinct forms in which matter can exist.
A partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions and photons; the fourth state of matter.
A highly compressed state that shows properties of both gases and liquids.
A state with properties between those of conventional liquids and crystalline solids.
A two-dimensional crystal; a single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal pattern.
A state of matter that is not commonly encountered, e.g. dark matter or Bose–Einstein condensate.
A pure substance containing the same kind of atoms; the simplest form of matter.
A pure substance of two or more different elements combined in a fixed ratio.
Two or more elements or compounds mixed in any ratio, each keeping its own properties.
A mixture with a uniform concentration throughout, e.g. salt solution in water.
A mixture whose concentration differs in different parts, e.g. a sample of rock.
The existence of an element in more than one structural form.
A large molecule made by linking together a series of building blocks.
A mixture in which solute particles are completely homogenized in the solvent.
A mixture whose particles are slightly bigger than those of a true solution and do not settle down.
A mixture whose particles do not dissolve, can be seen and settle down on standing.
A solution that can dissolve more solute at a particular temperature.
A solution holding the maximum amount of solute at a particular temperature.
The amount of solute that can dissolve in 100 g of a solvent at a particular temperature.

examTips: Learn the 11 branches in book order: physical, inorganic, organic, environmental, analytical, bio-, nuclear, polymer, geo-, medicinal, astro-chemistry.
Remember earth = solids, air = gases, sea = liquids, sky = plasma.
Solid: definite shape and volume, needs no container. Liquid: closely attached, moves randomly. Gas: very widely apart, easily compressible.
Plasma is the fourth state and is found in fluorescent tubes, lightning and welding arcs; most matter in the universe is plasma.
Compound = fixed ratio, split by a chemical reaction. Mixture = any ratio, separated by physical methods. In water, H : O = 1 : 8 by weight.
Carbon has three allotropes in this chapter: diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene C₆₀. Sulphur: rhombic and monoclinic. Oxygen: O₂ and O₃.
Filter paper test: true solution leaves no residue; colloid passes through without settling; suspension settles and leaves a residue.
Solubility is always measured per 100 g of solvent at a stated temperature (NaCl 36 g and sugar 203.9 g at 20 °C).
Most solids dissolve more in hot water, NaCl barely changes, and gases dissolve less when heated.
In MCQs on branches, link the keyword to the branch: reaction rates → physical, pollution → environmental, drugs → medicinal, radioactivity → nuclear.

options: Anything that has energy but no mass
Anything other than energy that has mass and occupies space
Only substances that can be seen

practiceQuestions.explanation: Matter is anything other than energy which carries weight (mass) and occupies volume (space).

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which branch of chemistry deals with the reactions taking place in the nucleus of an atom?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nuclear chemistry deals with the reactions taking place in the nucleus of an atom.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which state of matter can be considered a partially ionized gas?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Plasma is a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions and photons.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which substance is the simplest form of matter, containing only one kind of atom?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An element is a pure substance containing the same kind of atoms; it is the simplest form of matter.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which mixture leaves a residue on filter paper?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Chalk in water is a suspension; its particles settle and are collected as a residue.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which of these is NOT an allotropic form of carbon?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The allotropes of carbon are diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene; rhombic sulphur is an allotrope of sulphur.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In what ratio by weight are hydrogen and oxygen combined in water?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A compound has its elements in a fixed ratio; for water it is 1 : 8 by weight.

practiceQuestions.prompt: At 20 °C, 36 g of sodium chloride dissolves in 100 g of water. A student stirs 50 g of NaCl into 100 g of water at 20 °C. What happens?

options: 36 g dissolves and 14 g settles at the bottom

practiceQuestions.explanation: The solubility is 36 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C, so the solution becomes saturated and the extra 50 − 36 = 14 g stays undissolved.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Solids are the only state of matter that do not need a container for storage.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A solid has a definite shape and fixed volume, so it needs no container.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The solubility of gases in water increases as the temperature rises.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The solubility of gases in water decreases with the increase in temperature.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A mixture contains its components in a fixed ratio.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. A mixture can have its components in any ratio; a compound has a fixed ratio.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Graphene is a two-dimensional crystal made of carbon atoms.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The existence of an element in more than one structural form is called ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Different structural forms of an element are allotropic forms and the phenomenon is called allotropy.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A solution which can dissolve more solute at a particular temperature is called an ____ solution.
practiceQuestions.explanation: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute at that temperature.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Soda-water bottles are kept in a ____ so that carbon dioxide stays dissolved for longer.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gases are more soluble at low temperature, so cooling keeps CO₂ dissolved longer.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the steps for preparing a saturated sugar solution in the correct order.

items: Keep adding sugar; dissolving becomes more difficult
Take about 100 g of water in a beaker
Extra sugar settles at the bottom of the beaker
Add 5 g of table sugar and stir; it dissolves
At one stage no more sugar dissolves (saturated solution)
Add another 5 g of sugar and stir; it also dissolves (unsaturated solution)
correctOrder: Take about 100 g of water in a beaker
Add 5 g of table sugar and stir; it dissolves
Add another 5 g of sugar and stir; it also dissolves (unsaturated solution)
Keep adding sugar; dissolving becomes more difficult
At one stage no more sugar dissolves (saturated solution)
Extra sugar settles at the bottom of the beaker

sequencingActivity.explanation: Take water, add sugar in portions while it still dissolves (unsaturated), and continue until no more dissolves; extra sugar then settles at the bottom and the solution is saturated.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A liquid has particles slightly bigger than those of a true solution. They cannot be seen, do not settle on standing, and pass through filter paper. What is it?
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: These are the properties of a colloidal solution such as starch solution or the white of an egg.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates a compound from a mixture?

options: A compound has its elements in a fixed ratio and is split only by a chemical reaction; a mixture can be separated by physical methods
A compound can be separated by physical methods; a mixture has a fixed ratio
Both have a fixed ratio of components and the same properties as their components
A compound keeps the properties of its elements; a mixture does not

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: A compound has a fixed ratio and needs a chemical reaction to break it; the components of a mixture keep their properties and are separated physically.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A hot saturated solution of potassium nitrate is cooled. What is the most likely result?

options: More KNO₃ dissolves because solubility rises on cooling
Nothing changes because KNO₃ is not affected by temperature
The KNO₃ turns into a gas
Crystals of pure KNO₃ separate because its solubility falls

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: The solubility of KNO₃ increases with temperature, so cooling lowers it and the extra solute separates as crystals.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A bottle of soda water is warmed. Which observation and reason are correct?

options: Bubbles escape because the solubility of a gas rises as temperature rises
Bubbles of CO₂ escape because the solubility of a gas falls as temperature rises
No bubbles form because gases are not soluble in water
More CO₂ dissolves because the water is hotter

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: The solubility of gases in water decreases when the temperature rises, so dissolved CO₂ comes out.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches an allotrope of carbon with its structure?

options: Graphite — spheres of pentagons and hexagons; fullerene — layers of hexagonal rings
Diamond — layers of hexagonal rings; graphite — giant macromolecule
Graphite — layers of hexagonal rings; fullerene — spheres of pentagons and hexagons
Fullerene — giant macromolecule; diamond — spheres of pentagons

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Graphite has layers of hexagonal carbon rings; C₆₀ fullerene has spheres of carbon atoms in pentagons and hexagons; diamond is a giant macromolecule.
